source.title: Variance-Preserving Initialization Schemes Improve Deep Network Training: But Which Variance is Preserved?

record.file_problem: The supplied text is the full paper; some equations and figures are flattened, and plotted values are not provided numerically.
record.tranche_reason: The paper compares data-dependent initialization schemes and reports their effect on training loss and speed, using a different method and measure from several claim versions.
record.gate_note: The paper reports initialization statistics and gradient magnitudes, but these are not themselves training-error results. The training-loss curves in Figure 4 are figure-only; the text explicitly states that scale+bias initialization improves training speed over scale initialization in each case. The text does not state a numerical final training error.
record.test_reason: The study directly compares training-loss trajectories under different initializations and with batch normalization. Its explicit speed results bear on V4; Figure 4 also tests V6, but the supplied text does not preserve readable batch-normalization comparisons.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors distinguish total from sample variance, show sample-variance decay under Kaiming initialization and its elimination by batch normalization, and report faster training with sample mean-variance-preserving initialization. They also emphasize that centering and sample-variance preservation produce exploding gradients in wide random ReLU MLPs.
record.recipe_differences: The study compares data-dependent per-layer weight scaling and per-feature bias centering, rather than the specific initialization families and depth tests listed in the claim versions.
record.method_sensitivity: Training speed comparison varies by architecture, dataset, and optimizer; the authors report the scale+bias speed gain in all tested cases.

fits_no_version.finding: Kaiming initialization preserves total variance while sample variance decays with depth; batch normalization eliminates this sample-variance decay at initialization.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Total-variance preservation can conceal loss of variation across inputs in deep randomly initialized ReLU networks.

fits_no_version.finding: In depth-50, width-3000 random ReLU MLPs, scale+bias initialization and batch normalization produce exploding backward gradients, with fitted log-squared-gradient slopes of -0.379 and -0.381 versus a prediction of -0.383.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Preserving sample variance at initialization can amplify backward gradients exponentially in wide ReLU MLPs.

record.problems: The training results are presented as plots without numerical loss values in the supplied text; each setting uses 3 random seeds. Final training classification error is not reported.
record.rows_left_out: None. Figure 4's four optimizer/architecture panels and three initialization schemes are represented in rows R1–R12.

untested.parts: Near-zero training classification error, corrupted or random labels, CIFAR-100, and size-dependent or regularization-dependent interpolation.
Teacher-student optimization, spurious local minima, and extra student neurons.
Training degradation with depth, matched plain versus residual comparisons, and special initialization of very deep plain networks.

Trainable-depth thresholds, activation-function comparisons, orthogonal versus Gaussian initialization, and very deep tanh or 10,000-layer convolutional training. The experiments do not establish that avoiding gradient explosion causes the speed gain.
Stability thresholds, catapult recovery, sharpness trajectories, and divergence.
Accuracy gain per iteration, higher-learning-rate tolerance, and Fixup residual-network comparisons. Searching for the fastest learning rate does not measure the maximum tolerable learning rate.

record.verdict_notes: The study is not an original source for these versions. No V6 verdict is justified from unreadable curves or the introductory citations. The initialization-statistics and gradient results do not independently establish training speed or trainable depth, and faster training with exploding gradients does not refute V4's stated sufficient condition. Figure 4 reports three-seed variability; learning rates were selected from optimizer-specific grids.

versions.untested_parts: CIFAR-10/CIFAR-100 training classification error, random or corrupted labels, model size, and long training.
Two-layer ReLU teacher-student problems, spurious minima, and student width relative to teacher width.
Plain versus residual network training error as depth increases; special deep plain-network training.

The paper tests data-dependent scale and scale+bias initializations on two convolutional tasks, not the listed initialization families, trainable-depth thresholds, or the very deep tanh and convolutional settings.
Training above a stability limit, loss rise and recovery, sharpness, and divergence.
Batch-normalization training speed is shown in Figure 4, but the text does not state its speed relative to the other schemes; learning-rate tolerance and accuracy are not reported as results.

relationships.condition: Data-dependent scale+bias versus scale-only initialization; ALL-CNN-C/CIFAR-10 and UNet/ISBI2012, each with SGD and Adam.
relationships.reason: R2, R5, R8, and R11 report faster training in every setting; Section 5.3 also states that their loss remains lower beyond 10,000 iterations. This supports initialization-dependent training speed.
relationships.display_finding: Scale-and-bias initialization trained faster than scale-only initialization in every tested setting and retained lower loss beyond 10,000 iterations.
